This guidance aims to align Canadian clinical laboratory data-sharing practices with international standards and improve diagnostic accuracy, equity, and innovation in genomic medicine. By emphasizing ethical principles, proportionality, and governance, it seeks to enable responsible data sharing; strengthen trust among patients, families, and professionals; and contribute to the broader global genomic data ecosystem.

papers.title: Comparison of Next-Generation Sequencing and Quantitative PCR Methodologies for Quantification of Fungicide Resistance in Mixed Samples of Colletotrichum siamense .
papers.abstract: Measuring the frequency of fungicide resistance alleles in pathogen populations is critical for understanding resistance spread and severity. TaqMan quantitative PCR (qPCR) is a standard method for allele quantification, whereas next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies offer an alternative for high-resolution detection. Because studies exploring NGS for this purpose are limited, the objective of this study was to compare the accuracy and feasibility of Illumina NGS amplicon sequencing with that of a previously validated TaqMan qPCR assay to quantify resistance alleles to thiophanate-methyl fungicide in a set of mixed Colletotrichum siamense DNA samples. For validation, a set with known frequencies of resistance to thiophanate-methyl was used as a control. Both the NGS- and qPCR-based methods were highly precise, with an R 2 of 0.99 and 0.97, respectively, for the C. siamense DNA samples with known resistance frequencies. However, with the samples of unknown resistance frequencies that were collected from detached blueberry fruit assays, the NGS method demonstrated more variability than the TaqMan method ( P < 0.001). This variability was likely associated with low target DNA concentration and the presence of host and nontarget fungal DNA, which reduced PCR efficiency. This study highlighted strengths and weaknesses of both technologies and important assay design considerations. It was concluded that NGS-based methodologies may be preferential for large sample sizes and for detecting multiple or novel mutations within a region, whereas the qPCR assay can be more efficient for rapid quantification of known alleles.

papers.title: TRACE: a framework for traceable biomedical resource construction demonstrated through single-cell glaucoma data
papers.abstract: The growing availability of public omics datasets presents opportunities for biomedical research, yet constructing research question-driven resources from distributed studies remains challenging due to heterogeneous data, incomplete metadata and limited documentation of curation decisions. Here, we present TRACE (Traceable Resource Assembly and Curation Ecosystem), a general framework that links systematic knowledge discovery, data curation and resource delivery while preserving provenance throughout resource construction. We demonstrate TRACE through TRACE-scGlaucoma, a curated single-cell transcriptomics resource for glaucoma and optic nerve biology. Systematic screening identified 57 eligible studies, of which 42 provided accessible datasets comprising approximately 3.3 million cells. The resource provides harmonised metadata, standardised cell-type annotations and reusable expression objects while retaining original study information and curation provenance. We demonstrate its analytical utility through cellular enrichment of glaucoma GWAS-associated genes, comparing candidate drug-repurposing signals across distinct biological contexts and assessment of cell-type annotation reliability. TRACE provides a systematic and traceable approach to transforming fragmented public datasets into reusable biomedical resources, supporting reproducible analyses and future extensions across disease areas and data modalities.

papers.title: FoldAbS: Repurposing the Protein Folding Model as a Foundation Encoder for Antibody Screening
papers.abstract: Therapeutic antibody screening requires prioritizing antibody candidates across specificity, affinity, and developability. Current pipelines typically silo these objectives and underuse structural information that governs antibody-antigen recognition. To address these inefficacies, we introduce FoldAbS, a unified supervised screening framework that reconceptualizes protein folding models as frozen foundation encoders, exploiting their internal representations to capture rich sequence, geometric, and interaction dynamics well beyond basic structure prediction. By coupling the folding model with lightweight, task-specific heads, FoldAbS seamlessly evaluates all three therapeutic criteria within a single architecture. Instantiating this framework with the open-source Protenix model (FoldAbS-Px) yields consistent improvements over baseline approaches, achieving significant performance gains of up to 13.1%, 9.2%, and 6.2% in specificity, affinity, and developability, respectively. Collectively, these results reposition protein folding models from structure predictors and confidence scorers into reusable foundation encoders for comprehensive and supervised antibody screening. Our code is available at https://github.com/nohandsomewujun/FoldAbS.

papers.title: Benchmarking Statistical Methods for Differential Composition Analysis in Population-Scale Single-Cell Data
papers.abstract: Population-scale single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data capture cellular composition across cohorts ranging from several dozen to thousands of individuals, enabling the detection of cell-type composition differences between conditions. These differences reveal cellular shifts in disease pathogenesis and suggest potential targets for therapeutic intervention. However, differential composition analysis in scRNA-seq data is challenged by the unique features of cell count data, such as compositionality, prevalence of zeros, overdispersion, and confounding by technical and biological covariates. While this analysis is routinely performed, no study has yet systematically evaluated existing methods. Here, we benchmarked 12 methods for differential composition analysis using three population-scale scRNA-seq datasets with diverse and representative characteristics. Analyses of real data revealed low agreement across methods, while permutations and simulations based on the real data demonstrated excessive false discoveries for most methods. Overall, LOCOM emerged as the top-performing method that controls the false discovery rate while maintaining good statistical power, followed by ANCOM-BC and linear regression with centered-log-ratio transformation. Integrating evidence from real-data analyses and data-informed permutation and simulation experiments, we provide practical guidance tailored to common real-world challenges in differential composition analysis.

papers.title: Translating chemical reactions into enzyme sequences enables formate dehydrogenase engineering
papers.abstract: Enzyme engineering has broad applications across chemistry and biotechnology but remains costly and susceptible to low success rates. Generative artificial intelligence can substantially expand the sequence space accessible to enzyme engineering; however, directing generation towards enzymes that catalyse a user-defined chemical reaction remains challenging. Inspired by machine translation, we formulate enzyme generation as translation between two molecular languages: chemical reactions and amino acid sequences. Here, we introduce REXzyme, a translation model that generates enzymes conditioned on user-defined reactions. First, we evaluate its designs using multiple in silico metrics and characterize the strengths and limitations of its generalisation capacity. Then, we steer REXzyme towards the generation of enhanced formate dehydrogenases for their reverse natural reaction, i.e., the reduction of carbon dioxide. All 20 generated enzymes were expressed and purified as soluble proteins and exhibited CO2-reduction activity, with the most active design reaching 2.5-fold the specific activity of the reference enzyme. Notably, all substitutions in the designed variants were performed on distal positions outside the catalytic site. Our results show that reaction-to-sequence translation provides a route for efficiently engineering enhanced biocatalysts.

papers.title: FeatureMAP enables network-guided interpretation of untargeted metabolomics
papers.abstract: Untargeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) metabolomics generates thousands of features, but incomplete metabolite annotation and reliance on predefined pathways limit their biological interpretation. Here we present FeatureMAP, an LC-MS feature-centric computational framework that integrates multi-evidence metabolite annotation, network-guided refinement, metabolic module discovery, and structured large language model-based functional interpretation. Across ten public datasets, FeatureMAP improved MS1-based metabolite candidate prioritization while reducing annotation redundancy. In semi-synthetic benchmarks, FeatureMAP recovered coordinated metabolic perturbations, achieving 92% recovery of a simulated perturbation, and distinguished concurrent metabolic processes. Controlled benchmarks further evaluated functional interpretation under competing metabolite-level signals. Based on FeatureMAP, we additionally developed PhenoMAP, a phenotype-aware knowledge graph comprising 12,929 dysregulated metabolic modules from 501 human metabolomics studies spanning 326 phenotypes. Module-level comparisons revealed reproducible metabolic similarities across independent studies and biologically supported relationships among phenotypes. Application to Alzheimer's disease cerebrospinal fluid and cellular datasets identified convergent membrane-lipid alterations and implicated galactose-linked glycosphingolipid remodeling. Together, FeatureMAP and PhenoMAP enable network-grounded interpretation of incompletely annotated LC-MS metabolomics data and systematic investigation of metabolic dysregulation across biological conditions.

papers.title: A protein language model for domain, functional site, and variant effect prediction
papers.abstract: Protein sequence databases are growing far faster than experimentally curated annotations, limiting functional interpretation of newly identified proteins and coding variants. We developed PALM, a protein annotation language model that jointly predicts domain and functional-site occurrence, while preserving overlapping and nested annotations through a soft-target objective. PALM integrates ESM2 with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), learned layer aggregation, and a bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) encoder. PALM was trained on ~15 million InterPro-annotated UniRef50 sequences spanning 17,951 domain and 1,383 site classes. Across 2.3 million held-out proteins, PALM achieved domain- and site-occurrence F1 scores of 0.941 and 0.877, respectively, and retained substantial performance in proteins with <20% sequence identity to the training and validation data. PALM also substantially outperformed ESM3 annotation baseline. Without training on variant-pathogenicity labels, PALM embedding disruption distinguished 151,823 ClinVar missense variants more accurately than ESM2 embedding disruption (AUROC 0.835 versus 0.710), and combining PALM embedding disruption with the ESM2 likelihood-ratio signal reached an AUROC of 0.877. The same combined zero-shot score outperformed AlphaMissense on a benchmark dataset on 128,161 missense variants, that were derived from literature but not present in ClinVar database. At the protein level, PALM embeddings showed stronger CATH-Gene3D superfamily organization than frozen ESM2 and ESM3 embeddings, and improved prediction of experimental activation and repression effects when combined with ESM2. In a downstream case study, we demonstrated the ability to use PALM-derived embedding as proxy of deep mutational scanning (DMS), showcasing the broad application of PALM. Together, PALM converts curated residue-level knowledge into transferable and mechanistically interpretable representations that connect protein sequence, function, and variant consequence.

papers.title: Protify: A Benchmarking Platform Revealing Task Dependence and Homology Leakage in Protein Language Model Evaluation
papers.abstract: Protein Language Models (pLMs) have become essential tools for computational protein analysis, and the rapid proliferation of architectures, training objectives, and pretraining corpora has produced a diverse and expanding model landscape. Evaluation practices, however, remain fragmented: studies use different datasets, preprocessing pipelines, and reporting conventions, so results rarely transfer between publications. Here we introduce Protify, an open-source platform that standardizes pLM benchmarking across zero-shot, supervised, and transferlearning settings through a unified, low-code interface. Protify currently supports 35 pretrained models and 61 curated datasets and it is easy to add custom versions of each. Leveraging Protify's high throughput pipelines, we benchmarked 23 models on ProteinGym, discovering that DPLM3B is currently the top-performing self-supervised encoder. Another large-scale supervised evaluation across 32 diverse tasks, spanning enzyme classification, gene ontology annotation, protein-protein interaction, subcellular localization, and other functional properties, found that no single pLM dominated: 14 different models took the top score on at least one dataset, and the margins between the best and second-best models fell within run-to-run variability. On enzyme optimal pH prediction, a general-purpose probe pipeline matched or exceeded EpHod, a specialized model selected from 11,550 training runs, after 50 hyperparameter trials (R2 = 0.482 versus 0.425). Under a homology-controlled split of the same data, every pooled-embedding probe collapsed to near-zero R2, and only a transformer probe over full residue embeddings recovered appreciable signal (R2 = 0.248). Model rankings therefore depend as much on evaluation design as on the models themselves. Protify makes those design choices explicit, controlled, and replayable, and is freely available at https://github.com/Gleghorn-Lab/Protify.

papers.title: Language-guided domain adaptation improves protein sequence rep-resentations for antimicrobial resistance analysis
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR), particularly antibiotic resistance in bacterial pathogens, complicates infectious disease management. Because bacterial resistance is often mediated by protein functions, including antibiotic inactivation and efflux, protein sequence analysis provides a molecular basis for digital AMR surveillance and therapeutic intervention. We developed BacLLM, a language guided protein representation framework that integrates annotation-derived functional knowledge into protein language model representations for AMR analysis in WHO priority bacterial pathogens. Through sequence enhancement, semantic enrichment of UniProt annotations, and cross modal contrastive learning, BacLLM transfers LLM encoded annotation priors into the sequence encoder. Compared with baselines, BacLLM provided more informative representations for resistance-gene identification and mechanism prediction, captured resistance associated mutational signals at single-residue resolution, and preserved taxonomic relationships not reflected by phenotype based clinical groupings. Moreover, BacLLM recovered resistance associated functional organization within a TolC-centered protein association network, prioritizing proteins with low sequence identity to TolC but predicted structural similarity to TolC. Extending from AMR characterization to therapeutic prioritization, BacLLM also improved strain-level phage host matching for phage therapy candidate prioritization. Together, these findings establish BacLLM as a protein representation framework supporting AMR surveillance, functional characterization, and therapeutic candidate prioritization.

papers.title: Towards Robust Automated Mouse Scratching Behavior Detection for Itch Research
papers.abstract: Quantification of mouse scratching behavior is essential for preclinical itch research. However, manual video annotation is labor-intensive, and automated detection remains challenging in terms of accuracy and generalizability. We present Scratch-AID+, a computational framework dedicated to automated mouse scratching detection, including a diverse and progressive set of model families and learning strategies: classic ResNet-based detectors, task-adaptive fine-tuning of video foundation models, and in-context learning of advanced multimodal large language models. To simulate real-world use cases, we benchmark on a public dataset containing annotated video recordings from a source laboratory with additional cross-laboratory videos for independent testing, and we explore different data preprocessing and training configurations. We find that classic models suffer severe performance degradation on external data under our realistic setting with sparse scratching events. In contrast, fine-tuned video foundation models substantially improve the generalizability, achieving significantly better detection performance. Furthermore, frozen multimodal large language models demonstrate promising out-of-the-box ability using only few-shot demonstrations.We also report the effects of different video preprocessing strategies and ablations. Our findings highlight the improved performance and generalizability of the adapted foundation models for automated scratching behavior analysis and shed light on the real-world deployment of such detectors. Our code is publicly available at github.com/PennShenLab/scratch-aid-plus.

papers.title: Simple baselines rival protein language models in dense combinatorial protein landscapes
papers.abstract: Computational protein design demands generally applicable models that reliably predict or generate new variants with superior functional properties. A central test of this capability is whether models can extrapolate beyond the mutational regimes represented in their training data. Recent benchmarks have begun to address this question, but the performance of protein language models (pLM) remains less well characterized in densely sampled combinatorial landscapes of protein function that are commonly explored in protein engineering and design. Here, we evaluate zero-shot scoring and supervised prediction across mutational orders, comparing widely used pLMs with simple mutation-identity and evolutionary baselines. We find no consistent advantage associated with pLM architecture or scale, and that pLMs do not consistently outperform conventional baselines. We examined pLM representations and found that much of their variation could be recovered from mutation-identity encoding alone, helping explain the strong performance of such encodings without pretraining. We further found little correspondence between pLM sensitivity to sequence background and experimentally measured functional epistasis. In combinatorial library selection, pLMs likewise showed no consistent advantage over evolutionary scoring. Together, these results indicate that greater pLM complexity does not necessarily improve prediction or experimental prioritization in combinatorial protein design.

papers.title: COSMOS: integrated vector-pathogen metagenomics for mosquito-borne disease
papers.abstract: By 2050, almost half of the global population will be at risk of mosquito-borne disease. Effective response requires monitoring both pathogen transmission and vector abundance, yet these are typically assessed using separate assays with limited taxonomic breadth. Here we present COSMOS (COmprehensive Sequencing for MOSquito-borne disease), a targeted metagenomics workflow designed to reconstruct pathogen genomes and mosquito community composition directly from mixed field-collected samples. Over three annual rounds of a major Australian surveillance program, we evaluated >120,000 mosquitoes in 219 traps, with 98.7% agreement with surveillance data across seven monitored arboviruses, and additional detections of Sindbis virus and the state's first detection of encephalitic Little Sussex virus. Of 137 viral detections, 101 yielded near-complete genomes (>90% coverage) at median 95x depth. Using an accompanying computational workflow, COSMOS quantified mosquito composition, matching entomological estimates of reported vector species (CCC 0.78-0.89). Joint analysis of virus and vector composition identified structured mosquito communities associated with spatial and temporal environmental variation, allowing the ecological context of arbovirus detections to be characterised. Detections during the Murray Valley encephalitis virus outbreak in 2023 were concentrated within a narrowly defined mosquito-community space corresponding to rural communities dominated by the inland S-AUS sub-lineage of Culex annulirostris. Integrated vector-pathogen metagenomics provides ecological and evolutionary context for arbovirus activity within a single scalable workflow for surveillance and outbreak response.

papers.title: Predicting dynamic expression patterns in budding yeast with a fungal DNA language model
papers.abstract: Predicting gene expression from DNA sequence remains challenging due to complex regulatory codes. We introduce a masked DNA language model pretrained on 165 fungal genomes related to budding yeast that learns conserved regulatory sequence motifs. Fine-tuning the LM on yeast RNA-seq data--including high-resolution transcriptional regulator induction time courses generated in this study--yielded Shorkie, a model that substantially improves gene expression prediction compared to baselines trained without self-supervision. Shorkie identified canonical transcription factor (TF) binding motifs and captured changes in their regulatory contributions across induction time courses. Furthermore, Shorkie accurately predicted variant effects, outperforming leading sequence-to-expression models in cis-eQTL classification and achieving high concordance with massively parallel reporter assays. Interpretability analyses revealed Shorkie's ability to resolve promoter dynamics, splicing signals, and temporal changes in regulatory motif usage. Together, these results support combining pretraining on related fungal genomes with RNA-seq fine-tuning to improve sequence-based prediction of gene expression in budding yeast and provide insights into noncoding variants.

papers.title: DiverScan: attention-guided exploratory analysis of animal behaviour across diverse comparative experiments
papers.abstract: High-throughput tracking yields rich time-series data of animal behaviour, yet extracting biological insight remains a bottleneck, even for simple control--treatment comparisons. Existing analyses struggle to pinpoint the multiple, nonlinearly intertwined differences hidden in the data and fail to generalise across diverse recording set-ups. Here we present DiverScan, a deep-learning framework for attention-guided exploratory analysis of behavioural time series. DiverScan disentangles condition-dependent behavioural differences by pairing a loss function tailored to data exploration with an attention-branch architecture, and highlights condition-specific behavioural features visually and with explanatory text generated by a large language model. DiverScan is validated on a synthetic benchmark and on datasets from seven laboratories spanning multiple species and both single- and multi-animal behaviour. Beyond recovering known phenotypes, we demonstrate that DiverScan helps researchers generate new hypotheses across these diverse datasets. Available as Jupyter notebooks with a graphical user interface and flexible input formats, DiverScan can integrate into existing behavioural-analysis pipelines.

papers.title: RNA-X: Modeling RNA interactions to design binder RNA and simultaneously target multiple molecules of different types
papers.abstract: RNA interactions with proteins, other RNA molecules, and DNA play essential roles in numerous cellular processes and underpin a wide range of therapeutic mechanisms. Consequently, modeling these interactions is critical for understanding biological systems and designing novel RNA-based therapeutics. However, designing RNA sequences that selectively and strongly bind to a specific target remains a major challenge due to the vast sequence space and the current limitations of experimental and computational methods. In this study, we introduce RNA-X, the first RNA interaction foundation model which is based on masked language modeling for representation learning, conditional RNA design, and optimization. For the first time, RNA-X enables (i) RNA design targeting not only proteins but also other RNA and DNA molecules, and (ii) simultaneous design against multiple targets. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that RNA-X generates RNA sequences with natural structural characteristics and surpasses state-of-the-art methods in protein targeting. We experimentally validate RNA-X in vitro, where a RNAX-designed RNA targeting the 5'UTR of the androgen receptor (AR) mRNA was shown to reduce both AR transcript and protein levels in prostate cancer cells. Using affinity predictors and molecular dynamics simulations, we further show that the model can design RNA molecules that (i) target therapeutically relevant molecules such as p53 and thrombin proteins, and (ii) bind to targets with no prior interaction data, such as PHF6 protein. As a proof of concept, we designed a novel guide RNA from scratch that simultaneously binds (i) to the DNA of a bacterium and (ii) to the Cas9 protein. The resulting design achieves a predicted binding energy comparable to that of the wild-type guide RNA reported in the Protein Data Bank. Despite having orders of magnitude fewer parameters than existing RNA foundation models, RNA-X produces representations that outperform them across diverse RNA interaction-related downstream tasks. The code and pretrained model are publicly available on GitHub.

papers.title: Auditory Evoked Potentials Differ from Controls and Correlate with Aspects of Cognition in Kabuki Syndrome and Rubinstein-Taybi Syndrome
papers.abstract: Objective Kabuki syndrome (KS) and Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome (RSTS) are two disorders caused by dysfunctional components of the epigenetic machinery and both result in intellectual disability. Mouse models of both KS and RSTS have seen reversal of cognitive impairment with epigenetic treatments. However, a great need exists for biomarkers in these disorders to improve the likelihood of successful clinical trials. This study aimed to investigate cortical auditory evoked potentials (AEPs) in KS and RSTS so that it could potentially be developed into a response biomarker in the future. Methods The amplitude of the N1-P2-N2 complex was measured for passive listening to monotonal auditory stimuli in individuals with KS, with RSTS, and typically developing controls. A standardized cognitive assessment battery was performed and specific subtests were correlated with AEP values. Results Groups differed significantly in P2, N2, and P2-N2 amplitude although RSTS was consistently more different from typically developing controls than was KS. The mid- to late-phase AEP components (P2 and N2) also correlate with cognition within and across these groups particularly with language whereas earlier components N1 and P2 correlate more with measures of executive functioning. Conclusion Late-phase components of AEPs differ in KS and RSTS from each other and from controls. KS and RSTS differ from controls in P2 and N2 amplitude in the same direction and both show a positive correlation between language and P2 amplitude and a negative correlation between language and N2 amplitude. Together they also show an association with N1 and P2 amplitude and executive functioning. Significance AEPs may turn out to be a valuable response biomarker in KS and RSTS individually and together.

papers.title: Endothelial protein C receptor is an entry receptor for Langya virus
papers.abstract: Langya virus (LayV) was recently discovered in infected individuals with febrile illness and classified as a Parahenipavirus, a group of poorly understood pathogens. LayV is distantly related to Nipah henipavirus which causes recurring outbreaks with case fatality rates reaching up to 90%. No vaccines or therapeutics are approved for use in humans for any parahenipavirus or henipavirus despite their broad geographic distribution and pandemic potential. Here, we discovered that human endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR) is an entry receptor for LayV and that the tetrameric LayV attachment glycoprotein (G) binds EPCR avidly. We reveal the molecular basis of LayV G recognition of the EPCR receptor and provide a blueprint of the determinants of receptor ortholog usage. We found that human and shrew EPCR orthologs promote cell entry of LayV and of the closely related Mojiang pseudoviruses. These results along with the detection of several Parahenipaviruses in shrews set these pathogens apart from Henipaviruses, which use Pteropid fruit bats as reservoir hosts. Our data support future surveillance efforts, by enabling prediction of EPCR utilization among newly discovered Parahenipaviruses, and the development and evaluation of countermeasures targeting this emerging group of human pathogens.

papers.title: RPFace: From biased structural benchmarks to generalizable RNA-protein interface prediction
papers.abstract: Modeling protein-RNA complexes with co-folding and docking methods is routine, yet these methods are evaluated on benchmarks whose composition mirrors the deposited structures on which they were trained or tuned, leaving open whether their reported performance reflects true generalization. Here, we focus the evaluation on the region that carries the biological signal: the binding interface. For the first time, we construct and release a fair benchmark that stratifies protein-RNA data into distinct structural and experimental groups, providing a more stringent test of generalization than aggregate averages. On this benchmark, we find that accuracy of detecting the binding site using co-folding methods is concentrated in ribosomal complexes and varies systematically with factors such as experimental modality. For docking methods, it is reliable only when the input conformations are already close to the bound state, and it is inconsistent across RNA classes. Both families of methods fail to transfer to in vivo CLIP experiments. To address this gap, we introduce RPFace, to the best of our knowledge the first model that jointly predicts the binding preference of every protein residue and every RNA nucleotide directly from sequence, requiring no experimental structure, template, or multiple sequence alignment. RPFace combines an ensemble of predicted secondary structures with a multi-modal embedding-enrichment scheme that fuses representations from RNA foundation models and structure prediction models. Unlike existing approaches, it is a very small and fast model that delivers stable performance across structural and experimental conditions, is robust to conformational change, and generalizes to in vivo datasets without extensive pretraining. As a result, RPFace matches the state-of-the-art methods on protein interfaces with no evolutionary information, and outperforms them on RNA interfaces, with the largest gains in zero-shot settings despite using only sequence information. The model, code, and data are available at Github.

papers.title: An expansive internal chemosensory system in the insect abdomen implicates Gustatory Receptors in diverse aspects of interoception
papers.abstract: Taste and olfactory receptors are gatekeepers that convey chemical information about the external environment. Their role in chemosensory systems has been extensively studied in several model system, which established their role in triggering discrete behavioral as well as physiological responses related to feeding and social interactions. Over time, cases of chemoreceptors expressed internally in organs not linked to the external chemosensory systems of taste and olfaction have been reported. Here, we present the existence of a complex internal chemosensory system in the abdomen of Drosophila melanogaster. We show that the adult fruit fly harbors a complex internal chemosensory system, composed of about 80 to 100 abdominal chemosensory neurons (ACSNs) expressing approximately 20 different Gustatory receptor (Gr) genes, including all sugar receptor and several members of the less conserved bitter receptor genes. The cells expressing specific Gr genes are stereotypically arranged along the entire circumference of the abdominal body wall, in proximity of muscle and fat layers. The ACSN fall into at least nine different subtypes based on co-expression analysis, projection trajectories into the Abdominal Ganglion (AG) and location of cell somata. Identification of different subpopulation of ASCNs expressing discrete combinations of Gr genes indicates that these receptor complexes have new, previously not considered roles in interoception, including monitoring of different nutrients, detection of cell metabolites and their byproducts and chemicals associated with pathogens.

papers.title: Towards an analytical framework for investigating the neurophysiological influence of social context in speech perception
papers.abstract: Social information plays an important role in everyday speech communication, yet existing neurophysiological approaches provide limited means of isolating its contribution during naturalistic speech perception. Here, we present an analytical framework that combines the large language model (LLM) Mistral-Instruct, fine-tuned on conversational language, and temporal response functions (TRFs) to investigate the influence of social context on word-level speech processing. The framework disentangles local context (LC) from speaker-specific social context (SC) when generating LLM-derived lexical expectation measures, enabling such predictions to be generated under either matching or mismatching speaker contexts for the same speech material. This provides a direct way of isolating the contribution of social information to lexical predictions. We first show that speaker-related social context carries information about speech register and conversational role beyond that available from previous local context alone by interrogating Mistral-Instruct. We then demonstrate that lexical expectations generated from socially congruent contexts produce small but reliable improvements in EEG prediction relative to expectations generated from incongruent social contexts. These effects were observed despite identical acoustic input and neural recordings, indicating that the influence of social context on lexical expectations explains dissociable variance in neural responses to speech. Together, these findings provide a proof of concept for using LLM-derived lexical expectations to isolate and measure the influence of social context on speech processing. More broadly, the proposed framework offers a flexible approach for generating and testing hypotheses about how different forms of contextual knowledge shape neural responses during naturalistic language comprehension.

papers.title: TailEnrich enables discovery of dysregulated genes through disease sample enrichment testing
papers.abstract: Identifying differentially expressed genes is fundamental to elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying complex diseases. However, in complex disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), the genes exhibiting dysregulated expression may vary among patient subsets, reflecting the heterogeneity of the underlying pathological processes. Consequently, pathogenic genes are profoundly dysregulated in only a subset of patients. Conventional differential expression tools, such as DESeq2 and edgeR, are primarily designed to detect population-level expression shifts and may have limited power to identify subgroup-specific dysregulation. To overcome this limitation, we developed TailEnrich, a novel computational method that discovers dysregulated genes within patient subsets. TailEnrich independently tests the extreme left (downregulated) or right (upregulated) tails of a gene's expression distribution for disease sample enrichment. We quantify this enrichment using a new metric, i.e. the PE (Percentage of Enriched disease samples) score. On simulated datasets, TailEnrich demonstrates markedly improved accuracy over DESeq2 and edgeR in identifying dysregulated genes specific to patient subsets. Applied to AD gene expression data, TailEnrich uncovers a distinct, biologically relevant set of genes within key pathological pathways that are missed by mean shift-based approaches. TailEnrich provides a novel method for identifying dysregulated genes, and readily extends to other omics data including genomic variants and proteomics to uncover pathogenic genes in complex diseases.

papers.title: CauloBrowser 2.0: an AI powered update
papers.abstract: CauloBrowser is a systems-biology database for Caulobacter crescentus that organizes the largest repository of experimental data for this model bacterium. The original CauloBrowser provided a web interface for accessing these data, but the growing number of experimental datasets and advances in AI chatbots motivated an updated resource. We developed CauloBrowser 2.0 (CauloBrowser.org) as an open-source application that broadens access to RNA-seq, microarray, ribosome profiling, Tn-seq, ChIP-seq, and genome annotation data. The CauloChat AI interface allows users to query these datasets in natural language, generate visualizations, and achieve complex biological insights. While the database is hosted freely on the web, users may also download the database and run it locally, reducing dependence on the web-hosted service and allowing laboratories to use compatible unpublished datasets. Altogether, CauloBrowser 2.0 provides a significant update for exploring diverse systems biology data in C. crescentus.

papers.title: Who leads Marburg virus research? Gender, geography and funding in authorship, 2008 to early 2023: a bibliometric baseline before the 2023-2025 outbreaks
papers.abstract: Introduction. Between 2023 and 2025, Marburg virus disease reached Equatorial Guinea, Tanzania, Rwanda and Ethiopia for the first time. WHO's 2025 Marburg research priorities make leadership of studies by local scientists a continuing goal. This study describes who led Marburg virus research before these outbreaks. Methods. I analysed 684 English-language Web of Science papers on Marburg virus published from 2008 to February 2023 (5,700 authorships). Gender was inferred from first names with Gender-API, papers about African countries were identified from their text, funders were harmonised by country and type, and themes were mapped to the WHO priorities. I used Wilson 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and logistic and negative binomial regression. Results. Women held 35.1% (95% CI 33.9-36.4) of authorships, 41.6% (37.9-45.4) of first-author and 19.6% (16.7-22.9) of last-author positions. Women last authors rose from 15.1% (2008-2012) to 23.2% (2018-2023). Only 14.6% of papers had an author based in Africa. Of 102 papers about an African country, 25.5% (18.0-34.7) had a first author and 23.5% (16.4-32.6) a last author from that country, below benchmarks for infectious-disease research in Africa. Women based in Africa were last author on 2 papers. Of funded papers, 69.0% acknowledged a US funder (24.0% a US defence agency) and 3.2% an African funder. WHO priorities on clinical care, outbreak trials, social science and capacity strengthening each appeared in fewer than 8% of papers. An apparent citation penalty for funded papers disappeared after adjustment (rate ratio 1.07, 0.87-1.33). Conclusions. Before the recent outbreaks, Marburg virus research was led mostly by men in senior positions and by researchers outside the affected countries, and was funded mainly by US agencies. This baseline can track whether recent African-led responses change who leads the field.

papers.title: Wastewater pathogen composition in Atlanta, GA prior to and during the 2026 FIFA World Cup
papers.abstract: Mass gatherings can have many impacts on public health, including facilitating the spread of infectious diseases. Alternative surveillance modalities, such as wastewater-based surveillance (WBS), can complement traditional clinical surveillance. We utilized WBS to examine the influence of the 2026 FIFA World Cup (FWC'26) on the range of infectious pathogens in Atlanta, GA surrounding matches held in the city. Samples (n = 102) were collected from three water reclamation facilities between April and July of 2026 (34 collection days) and tested using the BIOFIRE(R) WATCHFIRE Respiratory (19 targets) and Gastrointestinal (22 targets) PCR Pathogen Panels. Primary data analysis included a temporal comparison of wastewater pathogen profiles before (April 1 to June 10; n = 60) and during (June 15 to July 15; n = 30) the FWC'26 across the three facilities using a modified Poisson model with Bonferroni correction. There were no statistically significant differences in target detection between the two periods. Samples collected after the FWC'26 (July 20 to 29; n = 12) were included in a sensitivity analysis which showed a statistically significant increase in SARS-CoV-2 (RR = 3.21, 95% CI = 1.40-7.39; p = 0.01, p-adjusted = 0.048) during and after the tournament compared to before. However, this coincided with regional and national increases in SARS-CoV-2 detection in wastewater, suggesting ongoing community burden. Wide confidence intervals, lack of quantitative data, and limited data collection after the matches limit our conclusions. This study demonstrates the use of qualitative, multiplexed PCR assays for WBS during a mass gathering sporting event.

papers.title: Beyond Haploinsufficiency: Protein Domain and Variant Class Shape Language Outcomes in SYNGAP1-DEE
papers.abstract: Background SYNGAP1-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (SYNGAP1-DEE) is generally considered a haploinsufficiency disorder, yet language development varies considerably between affected individuals. With targeted therapies, including antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), approaching clinical evaluation, understanding genotype-specific differences is increasingly important. We investigated whether expressive language and functional communication are associated with SynGAP protein domains and variant class. Methods We analyzed cross-sectional caregiver-reported data linked to genetic reports from the international PATRE SYNGAP1 registry. Of 440 participants, 334 had variants that could be assigned to a protein domain and classified as missense (n=79) or truncating/splicing (n=255). Variants were mapped to seven predefined SynGAP protein regions. The primary outcome was a five-level current expressive language score. Secondary outcomes included acquisition of two-word phrases and CFCS-derived functional communication. Each domain was compared with all other regions within the same variant class using nonparametric tests and age-adjusted ordinal or logistic regression. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction was applied. Results Missense variants in the C2 domain (aa248-392; n=28) were associated with markedly poorer expressive language (median score 1 vs. 2; age-adjusted OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.06-0.46; q=0.0025). Only 7.1% had acquired two-word phrases compared with 52.0% of individuals with missense variants outside C2 (OR 0.07; q=0.0023). Functional communication was also significantly impaired (OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.09-0.56; q=0.0052). Conversely, truncating/splicing variants in the PH domain (aa103-247; n=50) were associated with better expressive language (median 3 vs. 2; OR 3.52, 95% CI 1.99-6.24; q<0.001) and more frequent acquisition of two-word phrases (62.0% vs. 31.5%). No corresponding language association was observed for C2 truncating/splicing variants or for variants in the RasGAP domain. Conclusions Language outcomes in SYNGAP1-DEE are associated with both variant class and protein location. The marked impairment associated with C2 missense variants contrasts with the relatively preserved language abilities observed in PH truncating/splicing variants, suggesting that SYNGAP1-related disease cannot be fully explained by a uniform haploinsufficiency model alone. These findings support considering protein domain and variant class in future ASO trials, particularly for patient stratification, endpoint selection, and interpretation of treatment outcomes.

papers.title: Figure format and the accuracy of AI-assisted reconstruction of Kaplan-Meier survival data
papers.abstract: Reconstructing participant-level data from published Kaplan-Meier curves supports meta-analysis and other secondary survival analyses when original trial records are unavailable. Researchers may use original PDF figures or screenshots, which can look alike but retain different information. We assessed how converting vector figures to images affects reconstruction by a language model that can inspect files and execute code. We generated 64 independent two-arm datasets across four scenarios combining 100 or 1,000 participants per arm with proportional or crossing hazards. Each figure was supplied as a native vector PDF and a matched 300-dpi PNG to Opus 5.5 through Claude Code under the same instructions. Outcomes compared reconstructed records with the original observed records: time-averaged absolute curve error through 24 months, error in the between-group restricted mean survival time difference, and error in the Cox log-hazard ratio. Native PDFs had lower curve error in all 64 completed pairs, including replacements for incomplete runs. Mean errors were 0.000029 and 0.1047 percentage points for PDF and PNG, respectively; the paired difference was -0.1047 (95% confidence interval, -0.1194 to -0.0909). PNG errors in the restricted mean survival time difference and log-hazard ratio were small: mean absolute errors were 0.0084 months and 0.0027. Lower resolution and compression increased curve errors; embedding unchanged pixels in a PDF did not restore vector accuracy. Some PNG runs exceeded the instructed revision limit, so results describe the implemented workflow rather than performance under a strictly enforced limit. Preserving vector information improved reconstruction fidelity in this workflow, but the observed differences do not establish clinically consequential changes in treatment estimates. Validation against reported survival summaries and event counts remains necessary. Generalization to published clinical figures and other model workflows requires further evaluation.

papers.title: Multi-agent LLM teams improve differential recall on curated cases but underperform on emergency working-label matching: a two-cohort, two-family evaluation
papers.abstract: Background. Whether multi-agent large language model (LLM) pipelines help, add nothing, or underperform a single call may depend on the input and scoring contract rather than the architecture; these boundary conditions are unmapped. Methods. We compared a single direct call (Ax1), five personas in one context (P), and five isolated roles integrated by a moderator (MDT) across curated corpora (87 clinicopathological cases, 406 MedCaseReasoning cases, 392 replication vignettes) and two disjoint emergency cohorts from one repository (364 mixed-label encounters; a protocol-frozen 400-encounter disease-label-only replacement, one local serving stack). Scoring was judge-mediated top-k working-label matching. A completed factorial isolated the active ingredient; a symptom-permissive output-contract arm tested contract fit; three physicians rated discordant cases. Findings. On curated corpora MDT improved differential-list recall (top-3: +5.5 points, p = 0.0079; +3.0, p = 0.0079; +3.3, p = 0.0013) but not top-1 accuracy; the factorial attributed the gain to independent generation plus moderated synthesis, not personas. On emergency presentations the sign reversed: in the disease-label-only cohort Ax1 led MDT at every endpoint (top-3 -5.2 points, 95% CI -8.0 to -2.4, p = 0.0008), a second family reproduced it, and bridged cases excluded the serving stack. A symptom-permissive contract shrank the deficit's point estimates by 52-75%, replacement-cohort intervals all spanning zero though remaining negative; the clause harmed no arm. Physician safety ratings were inconclusive (original-cohort gate missed; replacement-cohort rescue contrast unadjudicable, 95% CI -32.7 to +2.6). Interpretation. Multi-agent diagnostic gains are real but conditional: the sign of the effect tracks input genre, and its magnitude tracks output-contract fit. Curated-benchmark gains should not be extrapolated to first-contact emergency text, where role-based teams underperform a single call at seven-fold token cost. The reversal is label-level and judge-mediated; clinical safety is neither established nor excluded.

papers.title: A Knowledge Database of Physical Activity Interventions for Hypertension using Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Physical exercise lowers blood pressure, but guidelines provide broad recommendations that rarely account for age, comorbidities, medications and hypertension severity. A structured, queryable resource of exercise interventions for hypertension is lacking, while manual curation is labor-intensive and difficult to scale. We present PAHD (Physical Activity for Hypertension Database), built with large language models (LLMs). An LLM screened 2,548 PubMed records through title-and-abstract and full-text assessment, selecting 255 studies. LLMs extracted arms, exercise protocols, participant characteristics, and outcomes, with two LLMs cross-checking study structure and each value linked to a verbatim quote. Programmatic integration generated 17,273 standardized records from 253 studies, one per reported comparison. Against adjudicated benchmarks, screening achieved 86.3% recall and 80.6% precision, and extraction 90.1% recall and 90.5% precision for blood pressure values. A clinician-facing portal retrieves studies matched to patients hypertension stage and comorbidities. PAHD is a reusable, traceable evidence resource for personalized exercise interventions in hypertension.

papers.title: Investigating pathways of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE) contamination and transmission in intensive care units: a prospective genomic surveillance study
papers.abstract: Background Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE) species are common healthcare-associated pathogens that cause difficult-to-treat infections. Whole genome sequencing of patients has revealed a substantial burden of patient-to-patient VRE transmission in hospitals, with patients in intensive care units (ICUs) at particularly high risk of acquisition. However, few studies adequately characterize the pathways of VRE transmission between patients in acute care settings - a necessary step to identify current gaps in infection prevention practices. By harnessing genomic clustering analyses of whole genome sequences of VRE isolates from patients, environmental surfaces, and healthcare providers (HCP) in ICUs, we aim to reconstruct indirect pathways of pathogen movement to identify patterns of VRE spread and opportunities for transmission prevention. Methods and Findings We collected daily samples (N = 6848) from ICUs in two hospitals over 13 weeks from four main sampling sources: patients, HCP hands, patient rooms, and shared surfaces. Samples were cultured on selective media and sent for whole genome sequencing (WGS). We used genomic thresholds to identify clusters of related VRE isolates and distinguish unrelated isolates. VRE was detected in samples from 20 out of 322 unique occupant-stays (6.22%). VRE isolates were detected from all sampling sources except for shared surfaces. A total of 44 unique VRE isolates were identified, 43 Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) and one Enterococcus faecalis (VREf). Two distinct patterns of VREfm spread were observed: 1) an outbreak setting with observed patient-to-patient transmission and low VRE genomic heterogeneity, and 2) high VRE genomic heterogeneity and pathogen movement between occupant-stays facilitated by persistent HCP and environmental contamination, but no observed transmission events. VRE detection probabilities were not significantly different between occupant-stays in outbreak and non-outbreak settings (OR = 0.63, 95% CI (0.23, 1.83), p = 0.32). However, including VRE isolates from non-patient samples increased the number of occupant-stays with VRE detection from 6 to 20, a 3.3-fold increase, as compared to patient samples alone. Including non-patient samples also increased the number of VRE multi-isolate genomic clusters detected by 7-fold. Our findings are limited because sampling was primarily conducted in ICUs. Due to the combination of short ICU stay durations and imperfect test sensitivity, VRE transmission events may have been underdetected. Conclusions Our findings characterize the complex nature of VRE transmission pathways in ICU settings. Even without an ongoing outbreak, we found substantial evidence of VRE movement between occupant-stays, facilitated by a combination of HCP hands and environmental surfaces. This study highlights the importance of environmental sampling for understanding VRE transmission potential, which is likely to be underestimated using patient sampling alone. We recommend that future studies incorporate follow-up sampling after discharge to better understand the true burden of transmission.

papers.title: Cognitive Performance in Prodromal Neuronal α Synuclein Disease
papers.abstract: Importance: Cognitive abnormalities may emerge during prodromal neuronal a-synuclein disease (NSD), but their domain specificity and longitudinal course are uncertain. Objective: To characterize baseline cognition and longitudinal change in prodromal NSD compared with healthy controls, NSD-negative genetic carriers, and sporadic Parkinson disease (PD). Design: Longitudinal cohort study using Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI) data, with first visits from July 2010 through April 2026 and up to 4 years of follow-up. Setting: Multicenter cohort. Participants: Healthy controls (HC; n=244), GBA1 or LRRK2 nonmanifesting carriers without NSD (n=323), prodromal NSD participants recruited through hyposmia or isolated rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder cohorts (n=1640), and sporadic PD (n=824). Exposures: NSD status and clinical cohort. Main Outcomes and Measures: Cognitive summary scores for verbal memory, executive function, processing speed, language, and visuospatial function, and PPMI-defined mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Models adjusted for age, sex, education, and APOE {varepsilon}4 status. Results: Among 3031 participants (mean [SD] age, 66.6 [7.0] years; 1322 female [43.6%]), prodromal NSD participants had lower baseline verbal-memory performance than HC (adjusted difference, -0.20 SD; 95% CI, -0.34 to -0.07; adjusted P = .007); NSD-negative genetic carriers did not differ from HC. No other cognitive domain was lower than HC at baseline or longitudinally. In the primary age-adjusted analysis, verbal-memory trajectory differed from HC over 4 years (P = .009), whereas in a smaller age-matched sensitivity subset through year 3, it did not (P = .62); the baseline difference persisted (adjusted difference, -0.28 SD; 95% CI, -0.46 to -0.10; P = .003). Adjusted MCI probability increased from 10.2% to 15.1% in prodromal NSD, compared with 8.4% to 5.0% in HC and 13.4% to 17.7% in PD. The increase was greater than in HC (ratio of annual odds ratios, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.04 to 1.58; adjusted P = .04) but not PD (P = .62). Conclusions and Relevance: Prodromal NSD was associated with modestly lower verbal memory and increasing MCI probability relative to HC, without lower performance in other cognitive domains. The baseline verbal-memory difference was robust, whereas the longitudinal trajectory finding was not reproduced in the smaller age-matched sensitivity subset.

papers.title: Benchmarking Structural Variant Detection in Whole-Exome Sequencing of 67 Multiple Myeloma Cell Lines
papers.abstract: Background. Although the majority of structural variant (SV) workflows have been derived based on whole genome sequencing (WGS) data, they continue to be applied to whole exome sequence (WES) data for which many studies have evaluated their performance in cancer. An equally important consideration that has not been well studied is the impact of cancer context specific features among WGS-derived SV callers applied to WES data. Similar to personalized medicine, not all SV callers are alike and optimal for use with all cancer types and sequence data types. In addition to sequencing related data features, cancer types have embedded features withing the sequencing data that should be considered. Herein, we performed an analysis of SV heterogeneity among WGS-derived SV callers to WES data in multiple myeloma (MM), a cancer known for its genetically heterogeneous nature. Using WES data derived from a panel of 67 Multiple Myeloma (MM) cell lines, we evaluated seven WGS-derived SV detection tools (Delly, SvABA, BreakDancer, Smoove, LUMPY and Manta) for their ability to identify cytogenetically known genetic abnormalities and to characterize overall differences in the number, length, type, and runtime of SVs called among them. Results. Among the seven tools, Smoove and Manta both had the shortest runtime, processing files in less than 2 minutes, in contrast to tools that required more than two hours to run such as SvABA and Pindel. Smoove was the only SV caller to identify a range of SV types, while SvABA was the most restrictive, calling only breakends. All tools differed in the length of SVs called, with SvABA's unfiltered output including the shortest length of less than 10 base pairs (bps), and Delly and BreakDancer's output including the longest, with SVs of less than 1,000 bps. At the chromosome level, SvABA's unfiltered output and Delly's output included 78% and 27.5% of known SVs, respectively, with the remaining tools (including SvABA's filtered output) achieved recall rates of less of less than 10%. By comparison, at the genomics coordinate level, no tool identified more than 20% of known SVs. Conclusions. As all evaluated SV detection tools achieved poor recall rates on this comprehensive catalog of MM cell lines, this study implies SVs detected by WGS-based SV callers on WES data should be confirmed experimentally before being declared legitimate. Heterogeneity in these tools' output lends support to their combined use in practice. Considering that many clinical grade sequencing panels continue to expand their repertoire of rearrangements with therapeutic implications, our results prompt the potential need for cancer type-matched workflows to evaluate the calling of such rearrangements.

papers.title: Agentic Pipeline for Large-Scale Clinical Data Queries in Enterprise Electronic Health Records
papers.abstract: Using electronic health record (EHR) data to answer clinical research questions is challenging. It requires understanding the research question, finding relevant information across different sources, and combining that information to produce meaningful results. We developed an agentic large language model (LLM) pipeline that decomposes investigator-authored requests into source-specific tasks, generates and executes SQL on EHR, integrates structured and unstructured EHR evidence, and applies study-specific clinical note adjudication. We evaluated this workflow against data analyst-identified cohorts across 50 pediatric orthopedic clinical data query requests. Of these, 43 were included in manual-review-adjusted performance analyses. The median adjusted positive predictive value, sensitivity among patients identified by either approach, and corresponding F1 score were 0.93 (95% CI, 0.88-0.98), 0.92 (95% CI, 0.90-0.95) and 0.90 (95% CI, 0.87-0.94), respectively. These findings support the feasibility of translating natural-language research intent into executable, autonomous multi-stage EHR workflows.

papers.title: EIN-RECAP: Evidence-Grounded Multi-Agent Summarization and Retrieval of Infectious-Disease Expert Discussions
papers.abstract: Infectious disease experts exchange practical knowledge through clinical discussions, but identifying relevant information across years of conversations is difficult. These discussions often contain differing opinions and emerging observations that are not yet reflected in published evidence. We present EIN-RECAP, an AI-assisted platform developed with Emerging Infections Network (EIN) experts and deployed in beta to summarize and search historical discussions. The system combines retrieval-grounded summarization, citation validation, and hybrid search while distinguishing published evidence from community experience. We evaluated summarization methods across 3,185 threads and conducted blinded expert review on a recent subset. Although a multi-agent workflow achieved stronger automated scores, experts favored a simpler generation pipeline and identified repetition, inaccuracies, and overconfident recommendations in the more complex system. This feedback motivated an ensemble that improved discussion coverage and key clinical points on nine high-disagreement threads, although retrieval relevance remained a limitation. Our findings demonstrate the importance of expert involvement in clinical AI development and show why automated evaluation alone is insufficient to guide system selection.
